summary: Defines mobility and multihoming extensions for HIP, including a general LOCATOR parameter with which a host tells peers other addresses where it can be reached. It also gives procedures for when a host changes its primary address. Multihoming procedures are left for further study. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 8046.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move to a new house, you tell friends your new address and still stay you. HIP hosts can do that without breaking conversations.

questions: how does hip handle address change
what is a locator in hip
how do hip hosts verify new addresses
subtitle: Let HIP hosts move to new addresses without breaking established connections.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol decouples identities from IP addresses, but hosts still need to notify peers when they move to a new address. There was no standard way to exchange new addresses and verify them.
tldr.mechanism: A LOCATOR parameter in HIP UPDATE messages allows a host to announce new addresses. The peer uses a nonce-based challenge (ECHO_REQUEST and ECHO_RESPONSE) to verify the host is actually reachable at the new address before using it fully.
tldr.outcome: HIP hosts can move between addresses or be multihomed, maintaining existing connections. The design is experimental and limited to basic mobility; more complex scenarios were left for future work. It was superseded by RFC 8046.

today: RFC 5206 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 8046, which provides updated mobility and multihoming procedures for HIP.

sections.title: Host Identity and Address Independence
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) separates host identities from IP addresses. In HIP, transport layer connections are bound to Host Identity Tags (HITs) and not to IP addresses. The HIP sublayer maintains the mapping between HITs and the current IP addresses. This design makes end-host mobility possible: a host can change its IP address while maintaining the same HIT, and the peer can continue to reach it.

However, for the peer to send packets to a host's new address, it must first be told about the address. RFC 5206 defines a LOCATOR parameter that allows a HIP host to announce new addresses to its peers. It also specifies procedures for verifying that the peer is actually reachable at the claimed address, preventing redirection attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Your real identity is your HIT, not your IP address. When you move, you just tell your friend your new IP address and prove you are really there.

sections.title: The LOCATOR Parameter
sections.content:
The LOCATOR parameter is a new HIP message parameter that carries one or more locator sub-parameters. Each locator specifies a point-of-attachment to the network, which is usually an IP address, but may include additional information such as an ESP Security Parameter Index (SPI) for multihoming scenarios. The parameter includes a Traffic Type field, Locator Type, Locator Lifetime, and a Preferred locator bit indicating which locator the host prefers to receive packets on.

A LOCATOR parameter with zero locator fields effectively deprecates all addresses. Hosts can send LOCATOR in UPDATE packets (the primary mechanism), or experimentally in R1, I2, or NOTIFY packets. The locators in the parameter must include all active locators for the host; this ensures the peer has a complete picture of reachability options.
sections.plainLanguage: The LOCATOR is a message that says "here are my addresses" and marks which one I prefer to be reached on.

sections.title: Mobility Without Rekeying
sections.content:
When a mobile host changes its IP address and does not rekey its security association, it sends an UPDATE message containing the new address in a LOCATOR parameter. The mobile host may also include an ESP_INFO parameter with both the old and new SPI values set to the current incoming SPI, signaling to any middleboxes that the address is changing.

Upon receiving the UPDATE, the peer validates it and performs address verification by sending back an UPDATE containing an ECHO_REQUEST with a nonce. The mobile host must reply with an ECHO_RESPONSE containing the same nonce. During verification, the peer marks the new address as UNVERIFIED and limits outbound data using Credit-Based Authorization. Once the peer receives the correct ECHO_RESPONSE, it marks the address as ACTIVE.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a message saying you moved. Your friend sends a challenge with a secret code. You echo it back, proving you are there. Your friend now uses your new address.

sections.title: Multihoming and Multiple Addresses
sections.content:
A host may have multiple addresses simultaneously for multihoming, such as multiple IPv6 prefixes or different interfaces. The host notifies its peer of additional addresses using the LOCATOR parameter. When multiple locators are in use, the host SHOULD indicate a Preferred locator that the peer should use for outbound traffic.

In multihoming scenarios, it is recommended that each address have its own Security Association (SPI) to avoid ESP anti-replay window violations. The host can set up a new SPI by sending an UPDATE with an ESP_INFO indicating a request for a new SA (OLD SPI set to zero, NEW SPI set to the new value) along with the LOCATOR parameter. The peer must perform address verification for each new address before using it.
sections.plainLanguage: You have multiple phone numbers. You tell your friend all of them and which one you prefer. Your friend verifies each number and calls you on whichever one makes sense.

sections.title: Address Verification and Credit-Based Authorization
sections.content:
Address verification is critical to prevent redirection attacks. When a peer receives a LOCATOR claiming a new address, it must verify the host is actually reachable there before sending full traffic. The verification is implemented using ECHO_REQUEST and ECHO_RESPONSE parameters containing a nonce. The host must echo back the nonce to prove receipt at the new address.

Credit-Based Authorization (CBA) allows the peer to send a limited amount of data to an UNVERIFIED address based on how much data has recently been received from that peer. This prevents amplification-based flooding attacks while the address is being verified. Credit is measured in bytes and decreases as the peer sends data to the unverified address. Once the address is verified (ACTIVE), credit limits are removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Your friend sends a secret code to the new address and checks if you can echo it back. While checking, your friend can send a little data but not a lot, to prevent attacks.

sections.title: Security Implications of Mobility
sections.content:
The design guards against three main security relationships: mobile node to peer, mobile node to home agent (not covered by this RFC), and mobile node to correspondent nodes. Impersonation attacks are prevented by the requirement that UPDATE messages be signed based on the host's identity. Denial-of-service attacks via packet redirection are mitigated by address verification and Credit-Based Authorization.

The RFC notes that mixed deployment environments where some hosts support HIP mobility and others do not require careful handling. Hosts that do not support HIP mobility will ignore LOCATOR parameters, which is safe because the old address remains valid. The ECHO_REQUEST/ECHO_RESPONSE mechanism ensures that address changes cannot be spoofed, as the peer can verify reachability before changing routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Your identity is proven by your signature on the message, not your address. Your friend verifies you can receive messages at the new address before trusting it.
